SynVesT-1 PET did not establish noninferiority to FDG PET

In 94 patients referred for cognitive-decline imaging, quantitative 18F-SynVesT-1 PET had lower AUC than 18F-FDG PET for AD (0.71 vs 0.81), and the prespecified noninferiority margin was not met.

SynVesT-1 PET did not establish noninferiority to FDG PET

In 94 patients referred for cognitive-decline imaging, quantitative 18F-SynVesT-1 PET had lower AUC than 18F-FDG PET for AD (0.71 vs 0.81), and the prespecified noninferiority margin was not met.

Key quantitative results: The cohort included 44 patients with AD, 12 with FTD, four with DLB, five with other neurodegenerative disorders, and 29 with non-neurodegenerative disorders.

BiomarkersFDG PETGlucose metabolismSynaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2ADifferential diagnosis

Added October 24, 2026 · DOI:10.2967/jnumed.126.272646; PMID:42914183

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The biologically appealing SV2A measure produced smaller neocortical effects and lower AD sensitivity than FDG. FTD visual performance was similar, but small subgroup sizes and quantitative AUCs still favored FDG. The negative noninferiority result is more decision-relevant than a simple statement that both tracers showed disease patterns.

Study design

Ninety-four patients referred for FDG PET also underwent 18F-SynVesT-1 PET/MRI a mean 49 days later. Median clinical follow-up of 11 months served as the diagnostic standard. Three-reader consensus and tracer-specific quantitative analyses were compared, with noninferiority defined by a lower 95% CI bound above a ΔAUC margin of -0.10.

Key quantitative results

  • The cohort included 44 patients with AD, 12 with FTD, four with DLB, five with other neurodegenerative disorders, and 29 with non-neurodegenerative disorders.
  • For AD, visual sensitivity was 0.57 with SynVesT-1 versus 0.73 with FDG; specificity was 0.76 for both.
  • Quantitative AD AUC was 0.71 for SynVesT-1 versus 0.81 for FDG; ΔAUC was -0.10 (95% CI, -0.21 to 0.01), so noninferiority was not established.
  • For FTD, visual sensitivity/specificity were 0.58/0.90 with SynVesT-1 and 0.50/0.93 with FDG; quantitative AUCs were 0.64 and 0.76 (ΔAUC -0.12; 95% CI, -0.27 to 0.04).
  • Posterior cingulate signal reduction in AD was about 10% with SynVesT-1 versus 20% with FDG.

What changed

A direct clinical comparison failed to show that synaptic-density PET could match FDG PET for the differential diagnosis of AD in this referral population.

Strength of evidence

Moderate negative clinical-validity evidence from prospective within-person imaging and blinded reader/quantitative comparisons. Precision is limited by the 94-patient single-center cohort, especially the small DLB and FTD subgroups, and the two scans were not simultaneous.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

FDG PET remains the better-supported functional imaging test for this diagnostic question; SynVesT-1 should not be positioned as a clinically interchangeable substitute based on these data.

Field medical relevance

Relevant to tracer comparability, visual versus quantitative performance, noninferiority interpretation, and the distinction between biological specificity and actual diagnostic performance.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The study compares an experimental synaptic-density tracer with routine FDG PET using three-reader visual assessment and quantitative analysis. SynVesT-1 is not an authorized AD diagnostic replacement and the data do not support substituting it for FDG PET.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No authorization, availability, reimbursement, or coverage change; the result argues against assuming an experimental tracer will reduce current FDG-PET access constraints.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Was SynVesT-1 noninferior to FDG for AD?
No. The confidence interval crossed the prespecified noninferiority boundary.
Did SynVesT-1 work better for FTD?
Visual sensitivity was numerically higher, but specificity was similar and quantitative AUC was lower; the 12-patient subgroup was too small for a firm superiority claim.
Is SynVesT-1 clinically authorized for this use?
No. It remains investigational.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Single tertiary center
  • Small diagnostic subgroups
  • Mean 49-day interval between scans
  • Median 11-month clinical follow-up rather than neuropathology
  • Experimental tracer availability
  • Noninferiority not established

Primary source · DOI
